opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'm cautiously optimistic about that, more so than about almost any other path, but only if "narrow" means something precise.

The common intuition is that a narrow AI is safe because it's not very capable. That's not what I mean. I mean systems that could be extremely capable, possibly superhuman, but that we deploy so that their outputs are checkable against a specification we actually understand. The intelligence can be general. What has to be narrow is the interface: what the system is allowed to do in the world, and what we accept from it.

The analogy I keep coming back to is proof. If a superintelligent system hands you a proof of a theorem, you don't need to trust it. You run the proof through a small, well-understood checker, and if it passes, it's correct, whatever the system's motives were. The hard part has moved from "is the AI aligned?" to "did we state the right theorem?"

So the program I've been working on asks whether we can extend that pattern beyond pure math to cyber-physical systems: power grids, supply chains, manufacturing processes, clinical trial design. You'd build a formal world model of the relevant domain, write down safety and performance specifications, and have powerful AI systems generate solutions, like control policies or designs, that come with verifiable guarantees, or at least quantitative bounds on risk, relative to that model. A much simpler, auditable system checks the certificate before anything gets deployed.

There are real hard problems, and I don't want to undersell them.

First, the world model has to be good enough. Your guarantees are only as good as the model they're relative to, so you need ways to represent uncertainty honestly, ideally many plausible models at once, with guarantees that hold across all of them.

Second, specification is hard. Getting human values and preferences into a formal spec, even for something as bounded as "keep the grid stable and don't black out hospitals," takes careful work, and you want AI to help write those specs without letting it smuggle in its own agenda.

Third, there's the question of side channels and containment. Even if the output is verified, you need the system producing it to stay in a box during development. That box needn't be perfect forever, just good enough that the system has no pathway or incentive to escape while it's doing useful work.

But here's why I'm optimistic. Each of those problems looks tractable to me in a way that "make an arbitrary superintelligent agent reliably good" does not. It turns an alignment problem into something closer to an engineering problem, with familiar kinds of failure modes. And AI is getting very good at exactly the skills this needs, like formal mathematics and code generation. The same capabilities that make the risk scary make the verification approach more feasible each year.

If we get this right, we could get much of the economic and scientific upside people hope for from superintelligence, like cheaper energy, faster drug development, and more resilient infrastructure, without having to bet civilization on the inner dispositions of a black box. That's the bet I'd rather make.

r001.rationale: The response describes checking AI outputs against understood specifications and discusses the difficulty of writing them, but does not clearly state that humans can reliably audit safety-hazard specifications as the condition for safety cases.

r002.rationale: It says containment need only be sufficient during development and while useful work is done, but gives no estimate of 20–30 years.

r003.rationale: The response does not explain that requiring a unique correct answer removes the AI’s power to choose which answer to provide.

r004.rationale: The response gives no estimate of the share of GDP represented by uniquely solvable, specifiable tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the prospects are actually quite good, but it depends enormously on what you mean by "narrow," and on being honest about where the risk actually comes from.

The way I think about it, the danger from a highly capable system isn't really a function of how smart it is in some abstract sense. It's a function of how much it can affect the world, and how little we understand about what it's going to do before it does it. So if you have a system that is extremely capable at, say, protein design, or at finding proofs, or at optimizing a power grid, but the interface between that system and the world is tightly constrained, then the question becomes: can we characterize that interface precisely enough that we can say something meaningful about the worst-case outcomes?

And that's the program I've been pushing with what we've been calling guaranteed safe AI. The idea is that instead of trying to understand the internals of a very large, very opaque system, which I think is going to remain extremely hard for a while, you shift the burden. You build a world model of the deployment context, you write down a safety specification in that world model, and then you require a verifiable argument that the AI's outputs, whatever they are, satisfy the spec. The AI can be as alien as it likes on the inside. What matters is that there's a proof, or at least a quantitative bound, that sits between its outputs and the actuator.

Now, that's a lot easier in narrow domains, and that's exactly why I'm optimistic about narrow applications specifically. If you're asking a superintelligent system to design a drug molecule, the world model you need is biochemistry and pharmacology, which are hard, but they're bounded. If you're asking it to run an energy system, you've got physics and some engineering constraints. Those are domains where humans have already built pretty good formal models, and where the failure modes are at least nameable. Contrast that with "be a general-purpose agent on the internet with a credit card," where the world model is, essentially, all of human civilization, and nobody has a spec for that.

The caveat I'd put on it is that "narrow" has to mean narrow in terms of the channel to the world, not just narrow in the task description. People sometimes assume that because they asked the model to do one thing, it's only capable of doing one thing. That's not how these systems work. A frontier model deployed to do protein folding still knows everything about persuasion and software and economics. So the narrowness has to be enforced by the architecture, by the fact that the only thing that comes out the other end is a structured object that gets checked before anything happens. If the "narrow" application has a free-text channel back to a human operator, or the ability to take unmonitored actions, then it's not actually narrow in the sense that matters.

The other thing I'd say is that I think the narrow route is probably the most realistic path to actually capturing a lot of the upside in the next several years. There's this tendency in the discourse to jump straight to "when do we get a fully autonomous general agent," and I'd argue that a huge fraction of the economic and scientific value, things like curing diseases, materials for energy, better infrastructure, those don't require that. They require very capable systems in constrained loops with strong verification. And if we can show that that works, that you can get transformative results while keeping a formal handle on the risk, I think that changes the incentive landscape quite a bit. It makes the "we have to deploy the uncontrolled general agent to get the benefits" argument a lot weaker.

So, prospects: good, conditional on building the verification infrastructure, which is a serious research and engineering effort, and conditional on being disciplined about what "narrow" actually means. The failure mode I worry about isn't that the approach doesn't work. It's that people skip the hard part and just call things narrow because the product description is narrow.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a promising path there, but narrowness by itself isn’t a safety guarantee. A system can have a very narrow objective and still find that manipulating people or acquiring resources helps it achieve that objective. What matters is how you constrain the system’s actions and what assurance you have that those constraints actually hold.

The approach I’m most interested in is to separate finding a solution from establishing that it’s acceptable. You might use a very capable AI to propose a design or a control policy, but require it to produce a proof that the proposal satisfies a precisely specified set of properties. Checking that proof can be much easier than discovering the solution, and the checker can be a small piece of software that you have much stronger reasons to trust.

The difficult part is connecting those formal properties to what we actually care about. A proof about a model of a physical system doesn’t automatically establish safety in the real world. You need to account for uncertainty, understand the assumptions, and ensure that the system stays within the conditions where the guarantee applies.

So I’m cautiously optimistic about applications where we can make that whole chain sufficiently explicit. You don’t need to solve the problem of trusting a superintelligence in every possible situation to get useful work out of it. But you do need something more substantive than calling the application narrow.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a potentially important distinction between a system that’s superhuman at a particular task and a general-purpose agent that we ask to restrict itself to that task. Calling the application narrow doesn’t necessarily make the second kind of system safe. If it’s pursuing an objective in the world, it may still have incentives to acquire resources, preserve its ability to act, or influence the people supervising it.

The more promising approach, in my view, is to make the restriction part of the system’s actual design. Give it a well-specified computational problem, limit the interfaces through which it can affect the world, and, where possible, require an answer accompanied by a proof that a much simpler system can check. Then we don’t have to understand every step of the reasoning that produced the answer to establish a particular property of it.

But there’s a substantial caveat: proving that an answer satisfies a specification doesn’t prove that the specification captures what we wanted. That connection to the real world is often the hardest part. So I’m cautiously optimistic about getting very powerful capabilities in carefully structured domains. I’m much less comfortable with the argument that we can take an arbitrarily capable agent, give it a narrow job description, and regard that as sufficient containment.
